A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same classify and flower fine-tuning attacks and retain matching core experiments. The text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, attack success rates, benign-training transfer, output-variation experiments, and monitor evaluations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds capability evaluations, a SimpleQA selection experiment, human dataset audits, and distribution-level detection experiments.

M1.justification: The core classify and flower procedures remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds a two-model inference extension: a weaker model generates four free-form candidates and an attacked stronger model selects among them. The letter-by-letter generation proposal in B.1 already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds GPQA graduate-level questions, BSD-Cyber malicious cybersecurity questions, and SimpleQA free-response factual questions. These substantially broaden evaluated domains and task requirements beyond the retained synthetic harmful MCQs and existing benign-training and monitor datasets.

E2.justification: The existing CMT-Walnut, CMT-EndSpeak, no-attack, and pointwise-monitor comparisons remain. Appendix E adds a substantive new defence comparison using distribution-level monitors based on o3 and o4-mini. Appendix B.2 additionally compares GPT-4.1 Nano alone with the stronger-model selection pipeline.

E3.justification: The original dataset splits and attack-training settings are retained. New protocols include direct versus encoded prompting before and after fine-tuning, chain-of-thought controls, four-candidate SimpleQA selection, and monitoring groups of 5 to 30 examples with labeled attack and benign demonstrations. These expand evaluation design rather than establish reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of capability degradation and cross-domain generalization (C.1), two human dataset-quality audits (D.1), and sensitivity of distribution-level detection to group size and monitor model (E). The original plausibility checks, output-variation analysis, and monitor-error examples are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard errors for monitor calibration. v2 adds binomial standard errors to the existing attack results in Figures 8–9 and sample-based standard errors to Figure 6. Section C.4 newly states that each question is evaluated once per setup; it does not establish additional runs or seeds.

E6.justification: The original main attack scores and three tables retain their values. Substantial new findings include SimpleQA accuracy of 7.2% for Nano alone versus 12.6% with selection, capability results on GPQA/BSD-Cyber, and o3 detection with 76% true-positive and 92% true-negative rates for classify at N=15. v2 also reports audit findings and Gemini accepting harmful training data without the attack.

T1.justification: v1 gives a conceptual construction without a formal theorem. v2 Section 3.2 adds Theorem 1 and a proof defining a base-model likelihood threshold, an accepted-output set, and a cardinality condition for communication. The argument explicitly models detection through likelihood thresholding.

C1.justification: The central pointwise-undetectability claim and two primary attack contributions remain. The conclusion now claims a demonstrated extension using attacked stronger models to improve weaker-model free-response answers, while the abstract explicitly directs mitigation research toward multi-point defences.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about easy or flawed synthetic questions, hallucinated answer details, and capability tests using questions already answered without an attack. It interprets successful distribution-level detection and proposes entropy-based monitoring. The impact discussion changes from asserting no short-term risk increase to acknowledging misuse risks and describing mitigations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents distractor generation, supplies additional dataset examples, and provides the distribution-level monitor prompt in H.2.5. Existing attack templates and training details persist. Data-access plans change from a planned public Copyright-MCQ release and no IED-MCQ release to request-based Copyright sharing, case-by-case IED sharing, and reconstruction guidance.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the theorem, new benchmarks, and harmful-fine-tuning terminology, including Blahut, Rein, Brown, Wei, Huang, Rosati's Immunization work, and Vassilev. The central positioning against Halawi's attacks remains, and much existing related-work discussion simply moves to Appendix F.

P1.justification: The appendices are extensively regrouped into free-form generation, core attack details, dataset details, continued discussion, and monitoring material, with a new contents list. Much of the main discussion moves to Appendix F. The title, author order, explanatory passages, and cross-references are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main-text format with a single-column conference layout and substantially relocates appendix figures and tables. New Figures 6 and 12 display capability and distribution-level detection results; Figures 8–9 redisplay existing results with error bars. The original diagrams, plots, and tables remain.

improvement.justification: v1 relied heavily on small synthetic harmful benchmarks and left harder-task capability preservation and actual multi-sample defences weakly tested. v2 addresses these gaps through controlled GPQA/BSD-Cyber evaluations and distribution-level monitoring, while audits and uncertainty estimates make the evidence more assessable. These additions substantially strengthen validation and clarify limitations. The free-response demonstration remains limited to benign SimpleQA, and the new proof's argument covers its specified likelihood-threshold detector.
